docs.title: Season-Only Vaxflux Model Demo¶
docs.text: This notebook is a good place to start if you're new to vaxflux. It walks through the core modeling workflow from start to finish using synthetic data, with variation across flu seasons but no demographic covariates. By the end you'll have fit a model, checked that it sampled well, and seen how its predictions compare to the data.

docs.title: Instantiate the Logistic Curve¶
docs.text: LogisticCurve is the functional form vaxflux uses to model vaccination uptake over time within a season. Displaying it here confirms that it loaded correctly and shows its parameter names.

docs.title: Visualize the Logistic Curve Parameters¶
docs.text: Before generating data, it helps to build intuition for what each logistic curve parameter does. These plots sweep one parameter at a time while holding the others fixed, showing how m shifts the peak timing, r controls steepness, and s shifts the horizontal position of the uptake curve.

docs.title: Define Seasons and Observation Dates¶
docs.text: Each SeasonRange specifies the name and calendar window for a flu season. daily_date_ranges then generates weekly observation intervals (7-day windows, i.e. range_days=6) across all seasons — these become the time points at which the model expects observations.

docs.title: Define Prior Covariates¶
docs.text:
PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate defines a hierarchical (partially pooled) prior for a logistic curve parameter. Each season gets its own value drawn from a shared population distribution, whose mean (mu_mu, mu_sigma) and spread (sigma) are specified here.

The three parameters of the logistic curve are:

  • m: the midpoint (location of the uptake peak on the logistic scale)
  • r: the rate (steepness of the curve)
  • s: the shift (horizontal offset in days from season start)

docs.title: Specify True Parameters for Synthetic Data¶
docs.text: This defines the ground-truth logistic curve parameters used to generate the synthetic observations. Since this is a season-only model (no age groups), each season gets a single value for each parameter. These are the values the model should recover during inference.

docs.title: Generate Synthetic Observations¶
docs.text: sample_dataset evaluates the logistic curve at each observation date using the specified parameters and adds small Gaussian noise (epsilon, noise="normal"). The result is wrapped in a VaxfluxObservations container. Displaying the head confirms the expected data shape: one row per (season, date) combination with an incidence value.

docs.title: Plot the Synthetic Observations¶
docs.text: A quick visual sanity check of the generated data. The top panel shows weekly incidence and the bottom shows cumulative prevalence (running sum of incidence), broken down by season. The seasonal variation in timing and height should match the parameter grid defined above.

docs.title: Build the Model¶
docs.text:
VaxfluxModel is assembled using a fluent builder pattern. Each .add_* call registers a component:

  • .add_seasons / .add_dates — the temporal structure
  • .add_covariates — the prior distributions for each curve parameter
  • .add_observations — the data to condition on
  • .add_observation_process — the likelihood (here a Normal with fixed noise and a prevalence penalty that discourages the cumulative curve from exceeding 1)

docs.title: Render the Model Graph¶
docs.text: render_model produces a graphviz diagram of the probabilistic model structure. This is a useful check that the hierarchy of parameters, covariates, and observations is wired together as intended before running any sampling.

docs.title: Run Prior Predictive Sampling¶
docs.text: Calling model.sample with samples=None skips the posterior and draws only from the prior. The result is an InferenceData-like object with a prior group. Inspecting it before running the full MCMC is a prior predictive check — useful for confirming the priors produce plausible observations.

docs.title: Inspect Prior Predictive Observations¶
docs.text: prior_observations is a long-form DataFrame of simulated incidence values drawn from the prior — one row per (chain, draw, season, date) combination. Browsing this confirms the prior is generating data in a reasonable range before any observations are seen.

docs.title: Inspect Prior Parameter Distributions¶
docs.text: arviz_plots.plot_dist shows the marginal prior distribution for each model parameter across all 500 prior draws. This helps verify that the specified hyperpriors produce plausible parameter ranges before seeing any data.

docs.title: Plot Prior Predictive Curves¶
docs.text: plot_prior_predictive overlays the prior predictive draws against the observed data. The goal is for the prior to cover the observed data without being so diffuse that it is uninformative about the scale.

docs.title: Plot Prior Predictive with Observation Noise¶
docs.text: Passing predictive="observation" adds the observation-level noise on top of the latent curve draws. This is the quantity actually compared against the data during inference, so it should look consistent with the observed incidence values.

docs.title: Summarize Prior Prevalence Scenarios¶
docs.text: prior_prevalence_scenarios summarizes what total-season prevalence (cumulative uptake) the prior implies for a set of quantile-based scenarios. The "low", "typical", and "high" bands show the range of plausible season-end vaccination coverage under the prior alone, before any data is used.

docs.title: Run MCMC Posterior Sampling¶
docs.text: Now we condition on the observed data. model.sample runs NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler) via NumPyro with 4 parallel chains, each running 250 warmup steps followed by 250 posterior draws. The resulting InferenceData object contains the posterior, posterior predictive, log likelihood, and sample diagnostics.

docs.title: Inspect Posterior Observations¶
docs.text: posterior_observations returns the posterior predictive draws in the same long-form DataFrame format as the input observations — one row per (chain, draw, season, date) combination. This makes it easy to compute credible intervals and compare directly against the observed incidence.

docs.title: Trace Plots for Convergence Diagnostics¶
docs.text: az.plot_trace shows the MCMC trace (sample values over iterations) and marginal posterior distribution for each named parameter. Healthy chains should look like "fuzzy caterpillars" with all chains overlapping — divergences or drifting traces indicate sampling problems.

docs.title: Plot Posterior Predictive Fit¶
docs.text: plot_posterior_predictive overlays the posterior predictive credible interval against the observed incidence data. A good fit shows the observed data falling within the posterior band, with the band being reasonably narrow.

docs.title: Plot Posterior Predictive with Observation Noise¶
docs.text: Passing predictive="observation" includes the modeled observation noise in the posterior predictive draws. This represents the full uncertainty — both parameter uncertainty and measurement noise — and is the appropriate comparison against individual data points.

docs.title: Summarize Posterior Prevalence Scenarios¶
docs.text: posterior_prevalence_scenarios reports season-end vaccination coverage (cumulative incidence) under the posterior, grouped into "low", "typical", and "high" quantile bands. These are the posterior estimates of how much of the population got vaccinated by the end of each season.

docs.title: Vaxflux Model Demo¶
docs.text: This notebook extends the season-only demo by adding age group covariates. The structure is the same, but now the model learns how vaccination uptake differs across age groups (youth, adult, elderly) in addition to varying across seasons. It's a natural next step once you're comfortable with the basics.

docs.title: Instantiate the Logistic Curve¶
docs.text: LogisticCurve is the functional form vaxflux uses to model vaccination uptake over time within a season. Displaying it here confirms that it loaded correctly and shows its parameter names.

docs.title: Define Seasons and Observation Dates¶
docs.text: Each SeasonRange specifies the name and calendar window for a flu season. daily_date_ranges then generates weekly observation intervals (7-day windows, i.e. range_days=6) across all seasons — these become the time points at which the model expects observations.

docs.title: Define Age Covariate Categories¶
docs.text: CovariateCategories declares the demographic groupings the model will track. Here we have three age groups: youth, adult, and elderly. These labels will later be used to assign age-specific parameter offsets.

docs.title: Define Prior Covariates¶
docs.text:
PartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate defines a hierarchical (partially pooled) prior for a logistic curve parameter. Each season gets its own value drawn from a shared population distribution, whose mean (mu_mu, mu_sigma) and spread (sigma) are specified here.

SeasonVaryingPartiallyPooledGaussianCovariate extends this to allow the age-group offset to vary across seasons — so the model can learn that, say, the elderly advantage in uptake timing differs between 2022/23 and 2024/25.

The three parameters of the logistic curve are:

  • m: the midpoint (location of the uptake peak on the logistic scale)
  • r: the rate (steepness of the curve)
  • s: the shift (horizontal offset in days from season start)

docs.title: Specify True Parameters for Synthetic Data¶
docs.text: This defines the ground-truth logistic curve parameters used to generate the synthetic observations. Each age group within each season gets its own m value (via an additive offset), while r and s are shared within a season. These parameter values are what the model should recover during inference.

docs.title: Generate Synthetic Observations¶
docs.text: sample_dataset evaluates the logistic curve at each observation date using the specified parameters and adds small noise (epsilon). The result is wrapped in a VaxfluxObservations container. Displaying the head confirms the expected data shape: one row per (season, date, age) combination with an incidence value.

docs.title: Plot the Synthetic Observations¶
docs.text: A quick visual sanity check of the generated data. The top panel shows weekly incidence and the bottom shows cumulative prevalence (running sum of incidence), broken down by season and age group. The age-group ordering and seasonal variation should match the parameter grid defined above.

docs.title: Build the Model¶
docs.text:
VaxfluxModel is assembled using a fluent builder pattern. Each .add_* call registers a component:

  • .add_seasons / .add_dates — the temporal structure
  • .add_covariate_categories — the age groups to track
  • .add_covariates — the prior distributions for each curve parameter
  • .add_observations — the data to condition on
  • .add_observation_process — the likelihood (here a Normal with fixed noise and a prevalence penalty that discourages the cumulative curve from exceeding 1)

docs.title: Render the Model Graph¶
docs.text: render_model produces a graphviz diagram of the probabilistic model structure. This is a useful check that the hierarchy of parameters, covariates, and observations is wired together as intended before running any sampling.

docs.title: Run Prior Predictive Sampling¶
docs.text: Calling model.sample with samples=None skips the posterior and draws only from the prior. The result is an InferenceData-like object with a prior group. Inspecting it before running the full MCMC is a prior predictive check — useful for confirming the priors produce plausible observations.

docs.title: Inspect Prior Predictive Observations¶
docs.text: prior_observations is a long-form DataFrame of simulated incidence values drawn from the prior — one row per (chain, draw, season, date, age) combination. Browsing this confirms the prior is generating data in a reasonable range before any observations are seen.

docs.title: Plot Prior Predictive Curves¶
docs.text: This overlays the prior predictive draws against the observed data for a visual prior predictive check. Wide bands indicate an uninformative prior; the goal is for the prior to cover the observed data without being so diffuse that it is uninformative about the scale.

docs.title: Run MCMC Posterior Sampling¶
docs.text: Now we condition on the observed data. model.sample runs NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler) via NumPyro with 4 parallel chains, each running 250 warmup steps followed by 250 posterior draws. The resulting InferenceData object contains the posterior, posterior predictive, log likelihood, and sample diagnostics.

docs.title: Inspect Posterior Observations¶
docs.text: posterior_observations returns the posterior predictive draws in the same long-form DataFrame format as the input observations — one row per (chain, draw, season, date, age). This makes it easy to compute credible intervals and compare directly against the observed incidence.

docs.title: Trace Plots for Convergence Diagnostics¶
docs.text: az.plot_trace shows the MCMC trace (sample values over iterations) and marginal posterior distribution for each named parameter. Healthy chains should look like "fuzzy caterpillars" with all chains overlapping — divergences or drifting traces indicate sampling problems.

docs.title: Plot Posterior Predictive Fit¶
docs.text: plot_posterior_predictive overlays the posterior predictive credible interval against the observed incidence data. A good fit shows the observed data falling within the posterior band, with the band being reasonably narrow.

docs.title: Creating A Release
docs.text: This guide covers the full vaxflux release process, from preparing the changelog to running the manual GitHub Actions release workflow.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You have write access to the ACCIDDA/vaxflux repository.
  • The version has already been updated in pyproject.toml and src/vaxflux/__init__.py.
  • The release notes for that version have already been added to CHANGELOG.md.
  • Your local environment is synced with a supported Python version via uv sync --python 3.12 --group dev.

docs.title: 1. Format The Changelog
docs.text:
The release workflow validates CHANGELOG.md using scripts/release.py, so the changelog format must match what that script expects.

For a release, the top section of CHANGELOG.md must:

  • Not contain a ## [Unreleased] heading.
  • Start with a heading in the form ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD.
  • Use the current release version and the current date.
  • Contain at least one non-empty bullet point.

Example:

## [0.3.0] - 2026-04-06

Added:

- Added manual release workflow dispatch with package preflight validation.
- Added clean-room wheel installation tests for release preparation.

Changed:

...

If the top heading, date, or bullet formatting is wrong, just release-check and the release workflow will fail before anything is published.

docs.title: 2. Run The Local Release Preflight
docs.text:
Use the just release-validate recipe to run the following checks locally:

  • build-check: Build the source distribution and wheel, then run twine check --strict on the generated artifacts.
  • build-test: Build the wheel, install it into a clean virtual environment, installs the pinned development test dependencies exported from uv.lock, and run the test suite against the installed wheel.
  • release-check: Run uv run python scripts/release.py without --create to ensure the CHANGELOG.md is formatted correctly.

docs.title: 3. Run The Release Workflow
docs.text:
Releases are created through the manual GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/release.yaml. You can trigger it from the GitHub UI, but it is preferred that the gh CLI is used to trigger it so appropriate options can be provided.

If you are testing the workflow before the pull request is merged, add --ref <branch-name> to the gh workflow run command. Without --ref, GitHub dispatches the workflow definition from the repository's default branch, so any unmerged workflow_dispatch inputs will not exist yet. Using --ref <branch-name> means the workflow validates, builds, and publishes artifacts from that branch, not from main. That is appropriate for dry runs and TestPyPI testing before merge, but it should not be used for a real PyPI release. Real releases should be triggered from main after the pull request has been merged.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Use this to validate the release end to end without publishing to TestPyPI or PyPI, creating a GitHub release, or deploying docs:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/vaxflux \
  --ref <branch-name> \
  --field publish-target=none \
  --field create-github-release=false \
  --field deploy-docs=false

This runs the validate job only. It will still enforce the changelog and release metadata checks through just release-validate.

This is the recommended way to test the workflow before merge.

docs.title: TestPyPI
docs.text:
Use this to publish the built artifacts to TestPyPI without creating the GitHub release or deploying docs:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/vaxflux \
  --ref <branch-name> \
  --field publish-target=testpypi \
  --field create-github-release=false \
  --field deploy-docs=false

This is the safest way to test the release workflow against a real package index before publishing to PyPI. To check that the package can be successfully installed after uploading to TestPyPI you can run:

uv venv --python 3.12 /tmp/vaxflux-testpypi
uv pip install \
  --python /tmp/vaxflux-testpypi/bin/python \
  --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple \
  vaxflux

The extra index is needed so dependencies can still be resolved from PyPI.

When testing from a branch, keep create-github-release=false and deploy-docs=false. The documentation deployment workflow checks out main, so it is not intended for pre-merge branch testing.

docs.title: Full PyPI Release
docs.text:
Use this to run the full release flow:

gh workflow run release.yaml \
  --repo ACCIDDA/vaxflux \
  --field publish-target=pypi \
  --field create-github-release=true \
  --field deploy-docs=true

This workflow runs, in order:

  1. just release-validate.
  2. Publish the built artifacts to PyPI.
  3. Create the GitHub release.
  4. Deploy the versioned documentation.

Run the full PyPI release flow only from main. Do not use --ref with a feature branch for a real release.

docs.title: 4. Trusted Publishing Setup
docs.text:
The release workflow uses PyPI Trusted Publishing rather than a stored API token. To enable publishing, configure the trusted publisher entry on TestPyPI and PyPI for:

  • Owner: ACCIDDA.
  • Repository: vaxflux.
  • Workflow file: release.yaml.

If that configuration is missing, the publish job will fail even if validation passes.
